title: Three-Property Rule Strategy
name: Three-Property Rule Strategy
metaTitle: Three-Property Rule Strategy in Oklahoma City, OK
metaDescription: We help Oklahoma City investors build a three-property identification list where every candidate is genuinely viable, not merely technically qualified.

sections.html: The three-property rule is the simplest identification framework in a 1031 exchange, and for most Oklahoma City investors we work with, it's also the right one. Identify up to three properties of any value, and you're not boxed in by the aggregate-value ceiling the 200% rule imposes. The strategy question isn't whether the rule applies, it's which three properties actually deserve a spot on that list.

sections.heading: Why Three Slots Changes How You Shop
sections.html:
With unlimited value but only three slots, every candidate needs to be genuinely viable rather than a placeholder address thrown on the list to hit a number. That discipline means narrowing the Oklahoma City inventory available in your basis range down to three real contenders you've actually had walked, instead of casting a wide net and sorting it out later once the clock is already running.

We treat each slot as a real decision, not a formality, since a wasted slot on a weak candidate is a slot you can't use on something better.

sections.heading: Building a Three-Property List That Actually Holds Up
sections.html:
We build each list around a specific role for each slot, not three interchangeable options:

  • One primary target you're reasonably confident will close, based on your own walkthrough
  • One backup in a different submarket in case financing or title issues stall the primary
  • One reach candidate that only works if your basis comes in higher or lower than expected
  • Confirmation that no property was already under contract to someone else at time of identification
  • Written, dated identification delivered to your intermediary before day forty-five
  • A financing pre-check on all three so none is eliminated purely on lending grounds

That structure gives you real options if your primary target stalls, rather than a scramble to find a fourth candidate once the window has already closed.

sections.heading: When Three Slots Isn't Enough for What You're Trying to Do
sections.html: If you're diversifying across several smaller assets, say splitting one relinquished property into a handful of self-storage or retail pads, the 200% or 95% identification rules may fit your deal better than the three-property approach. We help you decide which framework matches your actual strategy before you lock a list under the wrong rule and find yourself short a slot midway through sourcing.

sections.heading: Matching the Rule to Oklahoma City's Thin Inventory Reality
sections.html:
Certain asset classes here, medical office and net lease in particular, carry thin inventory at any given time, which makes treating the three-property rule as three genuinely viable options matter more locally than it might in a deeper market. A list of three loosely qualified addresses doesn't protect you the way three properties you've actually vetted does, and thin inventory is exactly when that difference shows up.

We start sourcing candidates well before your relinquished property closes specifically because of that inventory reality, so your three slots reflect properties we've already walked rather than whatever happens to be listed the week your clock starts.

sections.heading: What Happens If All Three Fall Through
sections.html: There's generally no automatic extension if none of your three identified properties close within the 180-day exchange period, and the transaction typically becomes a taxable sale absent rare extraordinary circumstances. That's exactly why we push hard on backup candidate quality upfront rather than relying on having three names on a page to satisfy the requirement.

faqs.q: Can I add a fourth property to my list after using the three-property rule?
faqs.a: Only if you're still inside the 45-day identification window and formally revoke and resubmit your list. Once that window closes, the three properties on file are fixed, which is why we build in backup candidates from the start rather than assuming a revision will be possible once the deadline has passed.

faqs.q: Does the three-property rule limit the value of the replacement properties?
faqs.a: No, unlike the 200% rule, the three-property rule doesn't cap the total value of the properties identified, which is why it's the more flexible option for a single larger replacement purchase in Oklahoma City, even when that purchase runs well above your relinquished property's original basis and sale price combined.

faqs.q: What if two of my three properties are in the same submarket?
faqs.a: That's allowed, but we generally recommend at least one backup in a different submarket so a single local issue, like a shared title or permitting problem, doesn't take out two of your three candidates at once. Spreading candidates across corridors also gives you a genuine price comparison rather than three variations on the same block in the same part of the metro.

faqs.q: Is the three-property rule always better than the 200% rule?
faqs.a: Not always. If you're diversifying across several smaller properties rather than buying one or two larger ones, the 200% or 95% rules may give you more flexibility. We help you match the rule to your actual acquisition strategy rather than defaulting to whichever one is simplest, since the wrong choice can box you in for the rest of the exchange and limit your options later.

faqs.q: What happens if none of my three identified properties close?
faqs.a: If none close within your 180-day exchange period, the exchange generally fails and the sale of your relinquished property becomes taxable. Building genuinely viable backup candidates from the start is the main way to avoid that outcome, and it's why we push back on any list that leans on a single strong candidate and two weak ones instead of three real contenders.
